questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to live in an English-speaking country within Europe. I did some reseach on culture, cities and nature. I also researched the university's courses and clubs/societies to make sure I would be satisfied with both the academic and social outcomes together with the need to experience new things during my exchange.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I found most of the needed information online prior to arrival. I had a contact number to the person responsible for letting me in at the accommodation.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was an introduction day with information on courses, websites and contact persons. Irish students were responsible for short tours on Main campus. When I picked up my student ID, I also recieved a map over campus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It was difficult. Before I got an accommodation-offer from the international office of my home institution, I looked at potential places to live. Even though I started my research half a year before my arrival, most dormitory rooms were already booked. I signed up for multiple waiting lists, but during spring 2023, the international office reserved a room for me.
I recommend to start looking for accommodation as soon as possible - maybe even in January if you are going abroad in autumn. The pricing is high no matter what, so you should not turn anything down because of the rent. Even with the offer from the international office, the rent was wery expensive.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: In Cork, many off campus houses are located close to the university, and I never met anyone who had to walk for more than 25-30 minutes. I believe the rent is more expensive off campus but the buildings are also often newer than the accommodations on campus, and the Irish students are highly prioritized when it comes to housing on campus in Cork.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The housing was okay but very expensive.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I received an e-mail with instructions on how to use their online platforms on wich I had to create a log-in and enter some personal information. When I had done my part of the work, I receied an official admission letter.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could always contact the employees by writing an e-mail. Often they replied within the same day or the following day(s).

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Before my exchange only the course descriptions (and what semester they would be tought) from the year before were available. Not long before my exchange the correct course describtions were published and some of the courses I had considered were now not available in the autumn semester. I changed my expectations on the courses but after arriving in Cork I had to change courses again because there were changed made to the time tables of some courses. The courses I in the end registrered for were therefore somewhat different from my original plan.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
You have to be really flexible and make sure to have a handful of  courses that sound interesting in case the courses yoou want the most overlapping timetables (the timetables were published shortly before semester start).

The earlier you apply for admission at University College Cork, the earlier it is possible for you to sign up for their accommodation list. This is sent to you as an online survey together with your admission letter, and they distribute accommodation on first-come-first basis.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Just like anywhere else, how organized a course is depends on the course coordinator(s).

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I chose courses from first, secound, third and fourth year.
The first year couse was an introductory course in a field outside my normal studies.
The third and fouth year courses were academically appropriate levels.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: At UCPH we usually have TØ/classes where we, as students, are supposed to say a lot. I know that some courses related to eg sociology, politics and language have seminars but for me (a science-student) there were no such thing. A few of my courses had some practicals/lab-exercises but otherwise than that, the courses consisted of lectures.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Introductory Programming in Python
Introduction to Pharmacology
Neuropharmacology
Cell and Molecular Basis of Neurodegenerative disease
Fundamentals of Nutrition Part I
Aspects of Irish Folklore

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Cell and Molecular Basis of Neurodegenerative disease: Great teachers and good insight on Alzheimer's Disease and Parkinson's Disease. Note that a lot they say is new research and a lot of different theories are mentioned.

Neuropharmacology: Topics are fun to learn and the lecturers are good. There are a lot of drugs to memorize but the overall learning outcome is good.

Aspects of Irish Folklore: A couse made specifically for exchange students. The lecturer is good at telling and making the story the center of the lecture (and not the powerpoint presentation). Even if you miss a lecture or two, it is not a problem. The final grade is based on an essay on a topic you choose yourself from a list.

Introductory programming in python: a good course if you do not know any programming beforehand. The lectures can sometimes be a little slow in pace but the lab-exercises are directly related to the lectures and you learn a lot from doing the programming yourself.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: none

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Generally, the prices are similar to the the Danish market. Coffee is a little bit more affordable, but transportation and clothing as about the same.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There are a lot of clubs and societies. Most of them are free to participate in (but if you go in trips with the moutaineering club or surfing club, it will not be free).
It is also free to use the Mardyke Arena because you can enter with your student ID. They have a swimming pool, an outdoor athleticks track, gyms with varying training fascilities and studios for dancing.

There were also societies for creative people and societies for people who want to talk to people like themselves. Examples are the knitting society, the scribble society, neurodivergent society and many more.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to the club/society fair in the beginning of the semester and choose some to show up to. It is good fun and you are not obligated to return just because you were there once. It is just a good opportunity to try a lot of different sports of societies.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Plan some weekend to go in trips to other towns or out in nature.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: You notice small differences in culture, but overall the way of living is similar to the Danish.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Nothing was that challenging

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The Irish are talkative when you start a conversation with them. Also the many pubs, often with live music.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Cork is a small and safe city but to get the full impression of Ireland, take time and visit other cities/towns (bigger and smaller) - and if you enjoy hiking, it is definitely an experience to go hiking in the wetlands.
- Start seaching for accommodation as early as possible and be willing to just pay whatever it costs.
- Ypu have to be flexible and tolerant when it comes to UCC. They are often giving information last minute compared to UCPH (e.g. when it comes to course timetables and final exam dates)

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Transportation is cheaper with a student leap card. You have to order it online.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Generally just experiencing so much and meeting so many new people. Of couse you have to study, but there are plenty of time so go on adventures with your friends or show up to a club/society by yourself.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Generally to find yourself in a completely new situation: no friends or family around, a new educational system and a city you do not know. But if you are determined to meet people and dare to show up to different social event, it quickly turns into new routines with new friends.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
